## Where we are

This is a **remote** session — work through it at your own pace, submit the outcome by the deadline announced in class.

By S1 you already have:

- a git repo with a trivial script, committed
- one completed OpenCode session

By S2 you have:

- a small set of R/Python scripts (same task, both languages)
- a hand-written test for each, catching a bug the agent introduced

This session does **not** re-teach `git init` / `add` / `commit` / `diff` / `log` — you already did that in S1. Instead it asks a different question:

::: {.callout-tip}
## Objective
Your repo currently works for *you*, on *your* machine, today. Make it work for an agent, a stranger, and future-you — on a different machine, next year.
:::

That reframing is the point of S3: **version control and project layout are agent-compatibility infrastructure**, not just a personal undo button. An agent that opens your repo cold has no memory of the conversation where you explained what `analysis.R` does, where the data lives, or which model you were using when it worked. The repo itself has to carry that information.

## Why hardcoded paths break agent workflows

Open your S2 repo and look for lines like these:

```r
# R
df <- read.csv("/Users/yourname/Desktop/econ-course/data/houses.csv")
```

```python
# Python
df = pd.read_csv("/home/yourname/Desktop/econ-course/data/houses.csv")
```

This works exactly once: on your machine, in that exact location. It breaks the moment:

- you move the folder
- a classmate clones your repo
- an agent is asked to "run this project" from a fresh checkout — it will `cd` into the repo root and has no reason to know your home directory even exists
- you run it from CI (a server that has never seen your filesystem)

::: {.callout-warning}
## The agent angle specifically
When you hand a repo to an agent and say "run the pipeline," the agent infers structure from what it can see: file names, relative paths, a README. A hardcoded absolute path is not just non-portable — it's a piece of context the agent cannot reconstruct from the repo alone. It has to fail, notice the failure, and ask you where the data really is. That's a wasted round trip you can eliminate for free.
:::

**The fix — always resolve paths relative to the project root:**

```r
# R: use `here::here()` — finds project root via .Rproj / .git, no matter your working directory
library(here)
df <- read.csv(here("data", "houses.csv"))
```

```python
# Python: build paths relative to the file's own location
from pathlib import Path
DATA_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data"
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "houses.csv")
```

Ask your agent to grep your repo for absolute paths (`/Users`, `/home`, `C:\`) and fix every hit using one of the patterns above. Verify by running the scripts from a **different working directory** than usual — if they still work, you've actually fixed it.

## Standard project layout

There is no single "correct" layout, but there is a well-understood default that both humans and agents recognize on sight — because it's the same shape as thousands of repos in their training data:

```
your-project/
├── README.md          # what this is, how to run it, what to expect
├── AGENTS.md           # rules file for coding agents (see below)
├── .gitignore
├── data/               # raw + intermediate data (often partially gitignored)
├── R/  or  src/         # source code — functions, not just scripts
├── scripts/            # top-level "run this" entry points
├── tests/              # your S2 tests live here now
├── output/             # figures, tables — generated, not hand-edited
└── prompts/            # archived prompts/sessions (see below)
```

Why this matters for agent compatibility: an agent that sees a `tests/` folder will *look there first* before writing new tests, and is more likely to run the existing suite before declaring success. An agent that sees everything dumped flat in the repo root has no such signal and will guess — badly.

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise 1 — restructure your S2 repo
Move your S2 scripts and tests into this layout. Ask your agent to propose the move, then check its work:
- Do the scripts still run from the new locations?
- Do the tests still pass?
- Did any path silently break? (This is exactly the "where is this wrong, how do I check?" habit from S2 — apply it here.)
:::

## README discipline

A README is the first (and sometimes only) context an agent — or a stranger, or you in eight months — gets before touching your code. A good README for this course answers, in order:

1. **What is this?** One or two sentences.
2. **How do I run it?** The literal commands, in order, from a clean checkout.
3. **What should I see?** Expected output — so a wrong result is recognizable as wrong.
4. **What are the parts?** A one-line map of the folders above, if not obvious.
5. **What does this depend on?** R/Python version, packages, any external data.

What a README is **not**: a changelog, a diary of what you tried, or a copy of your code comments. Keep it short enough that an agent's context window doesn't have to spend most of its budget reading prose to find the one command it needs.

::: {.callout-important}
## Test it like an agent would
Ask your agent — in a **fresh session**, with no prior context of this project — to read only your README and try to run your pipeline. If it gets stuck, your README has a gap, not the agent.
:::

## Project-level agent config: the rules file

OpenCode (and most harnesses) look for a project-level instructions file — conventionally `AGENTS.md` at the repo root (some tools also read `CLAUDE.md`; check your harness's docs, but the pattern is the same). This is where you put standing instructions that would otherwise be re-typed into every prompt: conventions, things not to touch, how to run tests before declaring success.

A minimal `AGENTS.md` for a course project:

```markdown
# Agent instructions for this repo

## Stack
- R (>= 4.3) and Python (>= 3.11), see README for exact deps.

## Conventions
- No hardcoded absolute paths. Use `here::here()` in R,
  `Path(__file__)`-relative paths in Python.
- Every function in `R/` or `src/` should have a corresponding
  test in `tests/`.

## Before declaring a task done
- Run the test suite (`Rscript tests/run_all.R` or `pytest`) and
  confirm it passes. Do not just say tests would pass.

## Do not touch
- `data/raw/` is read-only — never overwrite raw source data.
```

This is not decoration. It's the difference between re-explaining your conventions in every single prompt and stating them once, durably, in a place every session of every harness will read automatically.

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise 2 — write your AGENTS.md
Write one for your S2 repo. Keep it short — a few bullet points, not a manifesto. Then start a fresh agent session and ask it to make some trivial change (e.g. add a comment). Check whether it actually followed a rule you set (e.g. did it run the tests before saying it was done?).
:::

## Model pinning

"It worked when I tried it" is not reproducible if you don't know *which model* you tried it with. Models get updated, deprecated, or silently change behavior between provider-side versions. For a research pipeline, treat the model as a dependency, exactly like a package version.

- Record, in your README or `AGENTS.md`, which model + provider you used to develop/validate the pipeline (e.g. `openrouter/deepseek-v3.2:free`, checked on 2026-09-20).
- If your harness supports pinning a specific model version in its config (rather than "whatever is default today"), do that for anything you intend to reproduce later.
- This matters most for S9 (cost) and S11 (reproducibility) — you're planting the flag now that will let you answer "did the pipeline change, or did the model change?" later in the course.

## Prompt archiving

Your git history records what your *code* looked like at each commit. It does not record what you *asked the agent* to get there. For a reproducibility-minded workflow, that's a gap: two researchers with the same repo but different prompts can get different code.

Adopt a simple habit: save the prompts that produced non-trivial changes.

```
prompts/
├── 2026-09-20-restructure-layout.md
└── 2026-09-20-add-agents-md.md
```

Each file: the prompt you gave, and optionally a one-line note on what you had to correct afterward (this doubles as material for your S11 checklist later). This does not need to be exhaustive — archive the prompts that mattered, not every "fix this typo."

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why bother
If your Data Editor (or your future self) asks "how did this script come to look like this?", `git log` answers "what changed." A prompt archive answers "why," in the agent-assisted world where "why" often means "what did I ask for."
:::

## Package structure as a reproducibility unit

*(This section absorbs the old standalone `09-R-packages.qmd` — package structure, not turned into its own session, because for this course the point isn't "how to publish to CRAN," it's "structure is what makes a project reproducible.")*

A package (R) or an installable module (Python) is the strict, tooling-enforced version of everything above: a declared list of dependencies, a fixed internal layout, and a built-in place for tests. You don't need to publish to CRAN or PyPI to benefit from the structure.

**R — minimal package skeleton:**

```r
library(devtools)
create_package("~/myproject")
use_git()          # already done in S1, but this is how a package wires it up
use_r("clean_data")     # creates R/clean_data.R
use_testthat()
use_test("clean_data")  # creates tests/testthat/test-clean_data.R
document()          # builds documentation from roxygen comments
check()              # runs R's own structural + test checks
```

**Python — minimal installable-module skeleton:**

```
myproject/
├── pyproject.toml     # declares deps + build system
├── src/myproject/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   └── clean_data.py
└── tests/
    └── test_clean_data.py
```

```bash
pip install -e .     # editable install — code changes are picked up immediately
pytest
```

The common thread in both: dependencies are **declared** (`DESCRIPTION` / `pyproject.toml`), not just "whatever happened to be installed on my machine," and tests live in a place both a human and an agent will look for them by convention. This is what makes a project a *unit* someone else (or an agent, or CI) can pick up and run — which is exactly this session's outcome.

::: {.callout-note}

Turn one small function from your S2 scripts into a minimal package/module using the skeleton above, with one test. This is a preview of the discipline, not a full package-publishing exercise — that depth (vignettes, `pkgdown`, GitHub Actions CI) is available in the [`r-pkgs`](https://r-pkgs.org) book if you want to go further on your own.
:::

## Deliverable

By the end of this session your S2 repo should have:

- [ ] no hardcoded absolute paths (checked by running from a different working directory)
- [ ] the standard layout (`README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `data/`, source folder, `tests/`)
- [ ] a README a stranger (or a fresh agent session) could follow cold
- [ ] an `AGENTS.md` with at least the conventions you actually want enforced
- [ ] a note (in README or `AGENTS.md`) of which model you used to build/validate it
- [ ] a `prompts/` folder with at least one archived prompt from this session

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points
- Version control only delivers on reproducibility if the *project*, not just the *code*, is portable — no hardcoded paths, declared dependencies, discoverable structure.
- A rules file (`AGENTS.md`) is durable context: write conventions once, have every agent session read them automatically.
- Model identity and prompts are part of your provenance record now — you'll need them in S9 and S11.
- Package structure is the strict version of "clean project layout" — useful even if you never publish anything.
:::
